L75.about: Four pieces for solo piano that evoke the elegance of an antique French court: a bold improvisatory Prélude, a wry, archaic Menuet, the celebrated ‘Clair de lune’, and a quick, staccato Passepied. The suite looks back to the dance forms of the French Baroque while already bending them with modal colours and gently blurred harmony.
L75.ctx: Debussy sketched the pieces around 1890, when he was still a little-known composer in his late twenties, and revised them extensively before publishing the suite in 1905, three years after Pelléas et Mélisande had made him famous. The title comes from the ‘masques et bergamasques’ of Verlaine’s poem ‘Clair de lune’, a phrase Debussy loved; the bergamasque was a rustic dance associated with Bergamo.
parts: Sweeping, improvisatory flourishes before a lyrical, dance-like central melody.
A mock-archaic minuet, sly and delicate, with a faintly modal flavour.
The famous nocturne, its floating melody named after Verlaine’s poem.
A brisk staccato dance in the old French style.
facts: ‘Clair de lune’ was originally called ‘Promenade sentimentale’.
The Passepied began life under the title ‘Pavane’.
The suite was published in 1905, long after most of it was written.

L75/1.about: The opening piece of the Suite bergamasque, a bold and improvisatory Prélude marked ‘Moderato (tempo rubato)’. Sweeping flourishes and spread chords give way to a lyrical, dance-like central melody, all coloured by modal harmony that steps outside the usual Romantic idiom.
L75/1.ctx: Written around 1890 and revised for the 1905 publication, the Prélude nods to the keyboard preludes of the Baroque while sounding unmistakably like Debussy. It sets the scene for the antique, masked world the suite’s title suggests.
facts: Marked ‘Moderato (tempo rubato)’.
It opens the Suite bergamasque, which ends with the Passepied.
Its title looks back to the preludes of the Baroque keyboard tradition.

L75/2.about: A minuet in the mock-archaic manner, marked Andantino: delicate, wry and slightly askew, its melody shaded by modal inflections that make the old dance sound faintly strange. It is one of Debussy’s early exercises in looking back at the French court tradition through a modern lens.
L75/2.ctx: Like the other pieces of the Suite bergamasque, the Menuet dates from around 1890 and was reworked before the suite appeared in 1905. The minuet was the emblematic dance of the old French court, and Debussy treats it with affectionate irony.
facts: Marked Andantino.
The minuet was the signature dance of the old French court.
It sits second in the Suite bergamasque, between the Prélude and ‘Clair de lune’.

L75/3.about: Debussy’s most famous piano piece, its title meaning ’Moonlight’, taken from a poem by Paul Verlaine. A hazy, floating melody drifts over rich, impressionistic harmony, evoking stillness and light rather than telling any literal story — emblematic of Debussy’s break from the more narrative or dramatic programme music of the nineteenth century.
L75/3.ctx: Composed around 1890 and substantially revised before its publication in 1905 as the third piece of the Suite bergamasque, itself named after a phrase from Verlaine’s poetry evoking masked figures at a moonlit, melancholy revel.
facts: Debussy’s single most famous piano piece.
Takes its title from a poem by Paul Verlaine.
The third piece of the Suite bergamasque.

L75/4.about: The closing piece of the Suite bergamasque, marked Allegretto ma non troppo: a quick, light dance in F-sharp minor over a steady staccato bass, its modal, pentatonic-tinged melody skipping along without ever quite settling. It ends the suite with a touch of wit and understatement.
L75/4.ctx: The passepied was a lively dance of Breton origin that was popular at the French court in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Debussy’s early version bore the title ‘Pavane’; he changed it when he revised the suite for publication in 1905.
facts: The passepied is a quick dance in triple time associated with Brittany.
Its first title was ‘Pavane’.
It closes the Suite bergamasque.

L113.about: Six witty, affectionate pieces that picture a child’s world of toys, lessons and games: a parody of dull finger exercises, a lumbering toy elephant, a doll’s serenade, dancing snow, a little shepherd, and a cakewalk. The music is simpler in surface than most of Debussy’s piano works but full of sly musical jokes and delicate colour.
L113.ctx: Debussy wrote the suite for his young daughter Claude-Emma, nicknamed Chouchou, who was born in 1905. He gave the pieces English titles, in keeping with the Parisian fashion for things English and with her English governess. The suite was published in 1908 and orchestrated by André Caplet in 1911. Chouchou died in 1919, a year after her father.
parts: A parody of finger exercises that keeps drifting into daydream.
A toy elephant’s heavy, sleepy lullaby.
A light, guitar-like serenade with a Spanish tinge.
Swirling flakes in delicate, repeated figures.
A lonely pipe melody in a quiet pastoral setting.
A syncopated cakewalk that mocks Wagner’s Tristan.
facts: Debussy gave the pieces English titles.
The dedication apologises to Chouchou for ‘what follows’.
André Caplet orchestrated the suite in 1911.

L113/1.about: A comic portrait of a child at practice. The piece begins with brisk, dutiful finger exercises in the manner of a technical study, then the pupil’s mind wanders into a dreamy, lyrical episode before the drill resumes and hurries to a confident close.
L113/1.ctx: The title alludes to Muzio Clementi’s Gradus ad Parnassum, the famous collection of piano studies that generations of pupils practised. Debussy, who disliked routine technical drill, turns the tradition into affectionate parody for his daughter’s suite.
facts: The title alludes to Clementi’s famous book of studies.
The first piece of Children’s Corner.
Debussy’s piano writing here gently mocks routine finger exercises.

L113/2.about: A slow, swaying lullaby for a toy elephant, with a heavy, lumbering bass and a quiet, sleepy melody in the upper register. The music grows drowsier and thinner until it fades away, as though the elephant has nodded off.
L113/2.ctx: ‘Jimbo’ is usually taken as a version of ‘Jumbo’, the famous circus and zoo elephant of the nineteenth century, and Chouchou is thought to have had a toy elephant. The piece is the second of the six in Children’s Corner.
facts: The second piece of Children’s Corner.
‘Jimbo’ is usually read as a version of ‘Jumbo’.
Marked Assez modéré.

L113/3.about: A delicate serenade addressed to a doll, its light, plucked-sounding accompaniment imitating a guitar and its melody carrying a faint Spanish inflection. The music is airy and precise, with a tiny, elegant flourish at the end.
L113/3.ctx: Here Debussy imagines the doll as a sophisticated lady being serenaded. Like other pieces in Children’s Corner, it combines nursery whimsy with the refined touch of the mature composer.
facts: Marked Allegretto ma non troppo.
The accompaniment imitates a plucked guitar.
The third piece of Children’s Corner.

L113/4.about: A swirling, shimmering piece in which snowflakes drift in delicate repeated notes beneath a wistful melody. A note of melancholy runs through it, as though a child were watching the snow from a window.
L113/4.ctx: Debussy’s piano writing here relies on soft pedal effects and constant, fine movement to give the impression of falling snow. It is the fourth piece of Children’s Corner.
facts: Marked Modérément animé.
Built on constant fine, repeated figures.
The fourth piece of Children’s Corner.

L113/5.about: A quiet pastoral piece for a toy shepherd, with a simple pipe-like melody, stretches of gentle harmony and a mood of calm and solitude. Its tune sounds improvised, as if played on a shepherd’s reed.
L113/5.ctx: The fifth piece of Children’s Corner, the shepherd is one of the toys Debussy imagined for his daughter. Its unhurried pastoral manner offers a moment of stillness before the closing cakewalk.
facts: Marked Très modéré.
The melody imitates a shepherd’s pipe.
It comes just before the suite’s comic finale.

L113/6.about: A playful, syncopated parody closing Debussy’s suite Children’s Corner, mimicking the American cakewalk dance craze then fashionable in Paris, and slyly quoting and mocking the opening motif of Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde in its jazzy central section.
L113/6.ctx: Composed 1906–08 as the last of the six pieces of Children’s Corner, which Debussy dedicated ’to my dear little Chouchou, with her father’s tender apologies for what follows’ — addressed to his young daughter, though the suite’s technical demands make it unlikely a small child could actually play it.
facts: Mimics the American cakewalk dance, then fashionable in Paris.
Playfully quotes and mocks the opening of Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde.
The last of the six pieces of Children’s Corner, dedicated to Debussy’s young daughter.

L100.about: Three impressionistic ‘prints’ of far-off places: the pentatonic bells and gongs of a Javanese pagoda, an evening in Granada built on a habanera rhythm, and rain falling on French gardens. Debussy uses the piano as a palette of colour and resonance, and the set is a cornerstone of his mature style.
L100.ctx: Written in the summer of 1903, the Estampes were dedicated to the painter Jacques-Émile Blanche, who had painted Debussy’s portrait. Debussy had heard a Javanese gamelan at the 1889 Paris Exposition and had barely visited Spain, yet Falla was struck by how truly the second piece captures Andalusia. The set was premiered by Ricardo Viñes in January 1904.
parts: Pentatonic gong and bell sonorities inspired by the Javanese gamelan.
A sultry habanera with strummed guitar effects.
Storm-lashed gardens woven from two French children’s songs.
facts: The first performance was given by Ricardo Viñes on 9 January 1904.
Jardins sous la pluie was encored at the premiere.
Debussy was inspired by the Javanese gamelan he heard in 1889.

L100/1.about: Titled ’Pagodas’, an evocation of Javanese gamelan music that Debussy had heard performed at the 1889 Paris Exposition Universelle, using pentatonic scales and layered, bell-like textures to suggest the sound world of Southeast Asian percussion orchestras.
L100/1.ctx: Composed in 1903 as the first piece of Estampes (’Prints’), a set of three pieces each evoking a different exotic locale; the gamelan music Debussy encountered at the 1889 Exposition left a lasting mark on his harmonic imagination, evident here and in several later works.
facts: Evokes Javanese gamelan music Debussy heard at the 1889 Paris Exposition.
The first piece of the set Estampes (’Prints’).
Uses pentatonic scales to suggest Southeast Asian percussion orchestras.

L100/2.about: A slow habanera evoking an evening in Granada, with nonchalant, swaying rhythms, a Moorish-sounding melody in the left hand, strumming guitar textures and sudden contrasts of energy and languor. It is a masterly picture of Spain by a composer who barely knew the country.
L100/2.ctx: Composed in the summer of 1903 as the second of the Estampes, the piece is marked ‘Mouvement de Habanera’. The habanera rhythm had been popular in French music since Chabrier. Manuel de Falla later marvelled at how convincingly Debussy caught the atmosphere of Andalusia without quoting any Spanish tune.
facts: Marked ‘Mouvement de Habanera’.
Debussy had hardly visited Spain.
Falla admired its truth to Andalusian atmosphere.

L100/3.about: ‘Gardens in the Rain’ is a brilliant toccata-like study of a downpour in a French garden, its fast, whirling figures broken by flashes of sunlight. Debussy weaves in two French children’s songs, ‘Nous n’irons plus au bois’ and ‘Dodo, l’enfant do’, as if remembered from childhood.
L100/3.ctx: The last of the Estampes, it is the piece that brings the set back from Asia and Spain to France. It was encored at the first performance, given by Ricardo Viñes in January 1904, and Debussy later reused its material in the orchestral Gigues.
facts: Quotes ‘Nous n’irons plus au bois’ and ‘Dodo, l’enfant do’.
Marked ‘Net et vif’.
Encored at its first performance.

L66.about: Two early, graceful pieces named for the flowing, ornamental lines of the arabesque. The first is dreamy and gently undulating; the second is playful and sparkling, in G major. Both are lighter and more conventionally tonal than Debussy’s mature style, yet they are among his best-loved short works.
L66.ctx: Composed when Debussy was in his mid-to-late twenties and published in 1891, the arabesques show a young composer still working within a late-Romantic idiom close to Massenet, with his own voice beginning to emerge in the fluid rhythms and delicate harmony.
parts: Flowing, undulating lines and shimmering arpeggios.
facts: Published in 1891.
The title refers to flowing ornamental designs.
Among Debussy’s most popular early pieces.

L66/1.about: An early, flowing work whose gently undulating melodic lines gave the pair of arabesques their title, evoking the decorative, curving lines of Islamic ornamental art. Lighter and more conventionally tonal than Debussy’s mature style, it remains one of his most popular short pieces.
L66/1.ctx: Composed in his mid-to-late twenties, before the harmonic innovations of his fully mature style, the piece shows Debussy still working within a late-Romantic idiom indebted to composers like Massenet, even as his individual voice begins to emerge.
facts: One of Debussy’s earliest widely popular works.
Its title refers to the decorative, curving lines of Islamic ornamental art.
Written before the harmonic innovations of his fully mature style.

L66/2.about: A light, playful piece in G major, marked Allegretto scherzando, full of staccato figures, quick changes of texture and a mood of good-humoured sparkle. It is less famous than the first Arabesque but just as charming, and shows Debussy’s early gift for grace and wit.
L66/2.ctx: The second of the two Arabesques, composed in the years around 1890 and published in 1891. It is a fine example of the early Debussy who was still writing within a recognisably Romantic salon tradition.
facts: Marked Allegretto scherzando.
The companion to the more famous first Arabesque.
Published in 1891.

L68.about: A gentle, wistfully melodic early piece that became unexpectedly popular decades after its composition, though Debussy himself later regarded it as a minor, hastily written work and was reportedly embarrassed by its commercial success.
L68.ctx: Composed in 1890 and published the same year, likely written quickly to meet a publisher’s commercial demand for an accessible salon piece, from a period before Debussy’s mature harmonic language had fully emerged.
facts: Debussy reportedly regarded it as a minor work despite its popularity.
Composed early in his career, before his mature style emerged.
Its gentle, songlike melody has made it one of his most popular early pieces.

L95.ded: Mlle M. W. de Romilly (Prélude), Mme E. Rouart (Sarabande), N. G. Coronio (Toccata)
L95.about: A suite in three movements: a brilliant, rhythmic Prélude, a slow Sarabande in gliding chords, and the fast Toccata. Debussy revives Baroque forms and gives them a modern harmonic language, and the suite is often seen as his first fully mature piano work.
L95.ctx: Debussy composed the pieces at different times between 1894 and 1901. The Sarabande, the earliest, was later orchestrated by Ravel. The suite was premiered by Ricardo Viñes at the Salle Érard in Paris on 11 January 1902. Each piece has its own dedicatee, including Yvonne Lerolle, who appears in a well-known Renoir painting.
parts: A brilliant, rhythmic opening built on bell-like sonorities.
A slow, noble dance in gliding parallel chords.
facts: Ravel orchestrated the Sarabande.
Premiered by Ricardo Viñes at the Salle Érard in 1902.
Each movement is dedicated to a different person.

L95/1.about: The opening of Pour le piano is a bold, virtuosic Prélude marked ‘Assez animé et très rythmé’. It begins with a ringing, bell-like theme in repeated notes before racing through toccata-like passages, with a cadenza-like flourish and touches of the whole-tone scale.
L95/1.ctx: Composed in 1901, when Debussy was at the height of his fame after Pelléas, the Prélude was dedicated to Mlle M. W. de Romilly. It launched the suite Pour le piano, which Ricardo Viñes premiered in January 1902.
facts: Dedicated to Mlle M. W. de Romilly.
Opens the three-movement suite Pour le piano.
Uses whole-tone scales as well as Baroque-style figuration.

L95/2.about: A slow, stately dance in C-sharp minor, marked ‘Avec une élégance grave et lente’. Rich, gliding parallel chords and a solemn, archaic melody give it the air of an old portrait, and it is one of Debussy’s most haunting slow pieces.
L95/2.ctx: The Sarabande is the earliest part of Pour le piano, sketched in 1894 and revised for publication in 1901. It is dedicated to Yvonne Lerolle (Madame E. Rouart), whom Renoir painted at the piano with her sister. Maurice Ravel later made an orchestral version of it.
facts: Ravel orchestrated it.
Dedicated to Mme E. Rouart, née Yvonne Lerolle.
Marked ‘Avec une élégance grave et lente’.

L95/3.about: A brilliant, relentlessly energetic moto perpetuo closing the suite Pour le piano, harking back, like the suite’s other two movements, to Baroque dance forms while filtering them through Debussy’s own harmonic language.
L95/3.ctx: Composed in 1901, part of a suite whose three movements — Prélude, Sarabande and this Toccata — pay homage to Baroque keyboard forms, reflecting a broader early-twentieth-century French interest in reviving and reinterpreting earlier national musical traditions.
facts: Closes the suite Pour le piano, which revisits Baroque dance forms.
One of Debussy’s most virtuosic and technically demanding pieces.
Part of an early-twentieth-century French revival of interest in Baroque forms.

L110.about: Three pieces that carry Debussy’s piano writing into new territory: the rippling ‘Reflets dans l’eau’, the solemn ‘Hommage à Rameau’ and the whirling ‘Mouvement’. Each is a study in sonority and colour, and together they make one of the cornerstones of musical Impressionism.
L110.ctx: Some of the ideas date back to 1901, and Debussy sent the titles to his publisher in 1903. The set was published in 1905, and Ricardo Viñes, the pianist for whom Debussy wrote so much, gave the premiere. Debussy’s writing here often needs three staves to show all the layers of sound.
parts: Light playing on the surface of moving water.
A solemn sarabande honouring the French Baroque master.
A whirling study in perpetual motion.
facts: Book 1 was published in 1905.
‘Reflets dans l’eau’ is its most famous piece.
Debussy played early versions to Ricardo Viñes in 1901.

L110/1.about: Titled ’Reflections in the Water’, a shimmering evocation of light playing on the surface of water, built from rippling figuration and washes of harmony that blur conventional distinctions between melody and accompaniment.
L110/1.ctx: Composed in 1904–05 as the first piece of Images, Book 1, from a period when Debussy was consolidating the harmonic and pianistic innovations that would define his mature style, moving further from traditional tonal structure toward pure colour and atmosphere.
facts: Depicts light reflecting on moving water.
The first piece of Images, Book 1.
One of the most celebrated examples of musical Impressionism.

L110/2.about: A slow, solemn tribute in the manner of a sarabande, built on rich, bell-like chords that recall the grand French tradition. Its stately opening moves through shifting colours, and the piece builds to a monumental climax before subsiding.
L110/2.ctx: Jean-Philippe Rameau was the great master of French Baroque opera and keyboard music, and Debussy revered him. At a time when the first complete edition of Rameau’s music was being prepared, the ‘Hommage à Rameau’ was Debussy’s tribute, and it appears as the second piece of Images, Book 1.
facts: A homage to the French Baroque master Rameau.
Marked ‘Lent et grave’.
The second piece of Images, Book 1.

L110/3.about: A fast, whirling piece marked ‘Animé’, built on constant, flickering triplets that seem to circle in place. Its mechanical energy and crisp, brilliant textures make it one of Debussy’s most virtuosic short pieces.
L110/3.ctx: Debussy played an early version of ‘Mouvement’ to Ricardo Viñes as early as December 1901. It was completed and published in 1905 as the third piece of Images, Book 1, and closes the set with an explosion of energy after the calm of the Hommage à Rameau.
facts: Debussy played an early version to Ricardo Viñes in 1901.
Marked ‘Animé’.
The third piece of Images, Book 1.

L111.ded: Alexandre Charpentier, Louis Laloy and Ricardo Viñes (one piece each)
L111.about: A second book of three atmospheric pieces: bells heard through rustling leaves, the moon sinking over a vanished temple, and darting goldfish. The layers of sound are so intricate that Debussy wrote much of the music on three staves, and the set pushes his piano language to new extremes of colour.
L111.ctx: Composed in 1907 and published in 1908, Book 2 is dedicated in turn to the sculptor Alexandre Charpentier, the critic and Asia specialist Louis Laloy, and the pianist Ricardo Viñes, who gave the first performance. The influence of the Javanese gamelan and of Japanese art is strong.
parts: No. 1: Cloches à travers les feuilles
Bells heard through rustling autumn leaves.
No. 2: Et la lune descend sur le temple qui fut
Moonlight over an ancient ruined temple.
Goldfish darting in a brilliant, glittering toccata.
facts: Debussy notated much of it on three staves.
Each piece has a different dedicatee.
‘Poissons d’or’ was inspired by Japanese art.

L111/1.about: ‘Bells through the Leaves’ blends pentatonic and whole-tone sonorities into overlapping ripples of sound, like bells at different distances heard through a screen of foliage. The music shifts gently between layers of resonance, with a sense of hushed distance.
L111/1.ctx: The opening piece of Images, Book 2, it is dedicated to the sculptor Alexandre Charpentier. The chiming, gong-like sonorities show the lasting influence of the Javanese gamelan Debussy had heard at the 1889 Exposition.
facts: Dedicated to Alexandre Charpentier.
Marked ‘Modérément animé’.
Uses pentatonic and whole-tone scales.

L111/2.about: ‘And the Moon Descends on the Temple That Was’ is a slow, hushed piece full of Eastern colour, with pentatonic melodies, bell-like chords and long silences. It suggests a moonlit ruin of a temple, remote and still.
L111/2.ctx: Dedicated to Louis Laloy, a friend of Debussy who wrote on Chinese music, the piece is said to owe its evocative title to him. It is the second piece of Images, Book 2 and one of the most exotic of Debussy’s piano works.
facts: Dedicated to Louis Laloy.
Marked ‘Lent’.
Draws on pentatonic, Eastern-sounding scales.

L111/3.about: ‘Goldfish’ is a glittering, virtuosic piece in which shimmering runs and sudden darts suggest fish flashing through water. Quicksilver textures alternate with moments of calm, and the piece ends with a burst of sparkling brilliance.
L111/3.ctx: Debussy is said to have been inspired by a Japanese lacquer panel showing golden carp that hung in his study. The piece is dedicated to Ricardo Viñes, who premiered it. It is the third piece of Images, Book 2.
facts: Dedicated to Ricardo Viñes.
Said to be inspired by a Japanese lacquer panel.
Marked ‘Animé’.

L106.about: Titled ’The Isle of Joy’, a brilliant, ecstatic single-movement showpiece said to have been inspired by Watteau’s painting L’Embarquement pour Cythère, depicting lovers departing for an island of pleasure. One of Debussy’s most technically demanding and exuberant piano works.
L106.ctx: Composed in 1903–04, during the period surrounding his opera Pelléas et Mélisande and his affair with Emma Bardac, who would later become his second wife — a personally turbulent time that coincided with some of his most sensuous, high-spirited music.
facts: Reportedly inspired by Watteau’s painting L’Embarquement pour Cythère.
Composed during the turbulent period of Debussy’s affair with his future second wife.
Among the most technically demanding of Debussy’s piano works.

L105.about: A fast, nervous piece, marked ‘Très vif et fantasque’, driven by a tarantella-like rhythm and constantly changing moods. The music flickers between shadow and light like a masked figure, with brittle staccato writing and sudden dark harmonies.
L105.ctx: Composed in July 1904, when Debussy was separating from his first wife, Lilly Texier, the piece has a grim edge beneath its dance rhythm. Debussy told the pianist Marguerite Long that it was not about Italian comedy but about the tragic side of existence. Ricardo Viñes premiered it at the Salle Pleyel in February 1905.
facts: Premiered by Ricardo Viñes in February 1905.
Debussy said it was not Italian comedy but ‘the tragic expression of existence’.
Marked ‘Très vif et fantasque’.

L121.about: ‘The More Than Slow’ is a sultry, languid waltz marked ‘Molto rubato con morbidezza’, an affectionate parody of the sentimental waltzes played by café orchestras. Its melody sways and hesitates, and the mood is wry rather than sentimental.
L121.ctx: Written in 1910, the piece captures the world of the Parisian café and salon, and it was one of Debussy’s most immediately popular short pieces. He also made an orchestral version of it.
facts: Marked ‘Molto rubato con morbidezza’.
Debussy also orchestrated it.
A parody of the café waltz.

L70.about: A lyrical early piece with a Slavic folk flavour, its broad, songlike melody and rich harmony recalling the Russian music that had fascinated Debussy in his youth. The mood is warm and romantic rather than impressionistic.
L70.ctx: First published in 1891 as ‘Ballade slave’ and reissued in 1903 under the simpler title ‘Ballade’. Debussy had travelled to Russia in the early 1880s as a household pianist for Nadezhda von Meck, and Russian and Gypsy music was heard in Paris at the 1889 Exposition.
facts: Originally called ‘Ballade slave’.
Reissued in 1903 as ‘Ballade’.
Reflects Debussy’s early interest in Russian music.

L82.about: A dreamy, salon-style nocturne in D-flat major, gentle and songlike, in the tradition of Chopin and Fauré. Its long-breathed melody and rich harmony look forward to the more fluid style Debussy would develop in the following years.
L82.ctx: The Nocturne dates from 1892, the year Debussy began his Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune. It was not published in his lifetime, and it belongs to the group of early piano pieces written for the salons of Paris.
facts: Not published in Debussy’s lifetime.
Written in 1892, the same year he began the Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune.
In the tradition of Chopin’s nocturnes.

L71.about: A charming salon waltz with an elegant, lilting melody and touches of Chopinesque ornament. It is a delicate, unpretentious piece, written in the popular Romantic manner that Debussy was soon to leave behind.
L71.ctx: Composed in 1890 and published the same year, the Valse romantique belongs to a group of early piano pieces, including the Ballade, the Danse and the Rêverie, that Debussy wrote as a young composer trying to establish himself in Paris.
facts: Published in 1890.
One of several early salon pieces Debussy wrote around 1890.
Shows the influence of Chopin’s waltzes.

L69.about: A lively, whirling tarantella-style dance with sparkling rhythms and a brilliant, virtuosic finish. It is one of the most energetic of Debussy’s early piano pieces.
L69.ctx: First published in 1891 as ‘Tarentelle styrienne’ and reissued in 1903 as ‘Danse’. Maurice Ravel orchestrated it in 1922, along with the Sarabande from Pour le piano.
facts: Originally called ‘Tarentelle styrienne’.
Ravel orchestrated it in 1922.
Reissued in 1903 as ‘Danse’.

L65.about: A suite of four charming pieces for piano duet: ‘En bateau’, ‘Cortège’, ‘Menuet’ and ‘Ballet’. The music is light, elegant and full of grace, with a Gallic charm that owes something to Fauré and Massenet.
L65.ctx: Debussy wrote the Petite Suite in the late 1880s and it was published in 1889. Two of its pieces take titles from poems in Verlaine’s Fêtes galantes. Henri Büsser made a popular orchestral version in 1907, and the suite has always been among Debussy’s most approachable works.
facts: The titles ‘En bateau’ and ‘Cortège’ come from Verlaine’s Fêtes galantes.
Henri Büsser orchestrated it in 1907.
Written for one piano, four hands.

L86.about: A hazy, sensuous orchestral tone poem inspired by a poem of Stéphane Mallarmé depicting a faun’s drowsy, half-remembered erotic reverie in the afternoon heat. Often considered the work that inaugurated musical Impressionism and, with it, the beginning of twentieth-century music, for its dissolution of clear harmonic direction, metre and thematic development in favour of pure atmosphere and colour.
L86.ctx: Composed in 1892–94, the piece grew out of Debussy’s long fascination with Mallarmé’s poetry and Symbolist aesthetics; the composer Pierre Boulez later called its flute opening the moment modern music began to ’wake’ from the constraints of the nineteenth century.
facts: Widely considered the founding work of musical Impressionism.
Inspired by a poem by Stéphane Mallarmé.
Pierre Boulez called its opening the moment modern music began.

L91.about: Three orchestral pieces that turn to atmosphere and colour rather than narrative: ‘Nuages’ (clouds), ‘Fêtes’ (festivals) and ‘Sirènes’ (sirens), the last with a wordless women’s chorus. Debussy said the title referred not to the form of the nocturne but to the impressions and effects of light that the word suggests.
L91.ctx: Debussy first conceived the work as a piece for solo violin and orchestra for the violinist Eugène Ysaÿe, then reworked it for orchestra alone. It was inspired in part by the paintings of James McNeill Whistler, who titled several works ‘Nocturne’. ‘Nuages’ and ‘Fêtes’ were first heard in December 1900 and the complete set in October 1901.
parts: Slow, drifting clouds, with a plaintive cor anglais theme.
A festival with a military procession passing through it.
The sea and its sirens, with a wordless women’s chorus.
facts: Originally planned as a work for violin and orchestra for Ysaÿe.
Inspired by Whistler’s paintings called ‘Nocturnes’.
‘Sirènes’ uses a wordless women’s chorus.

L109.about: Three symphonic sketches of the sea, in which Debussy paints dawn breaking over the water, the play of the waves, and a dialogue between wind and sea. The orchestra shimmers with constant, subtle colour and motion, and the piece is one of the supreme masterpieces of musical Impressionism.
L109.ctx: Debussy composed much of La Mer in Burgundy, far from the sea, and finished it in 1905, in a year when his private life was in turmoil after leaving his first wife for Emma Bardac. The first edition’s cover carried Hokusai’s ‘Great Wave off Kanagawa’. The premiere in Paris in October 1905 was poorly received, but the work soon became a repertory favourite.
parts: De l’aube à midi sur la mer
From the dark hush of dawn to the blazing sun of midday.
Shimmering, playful waves in light, quickly moving colours.
Dialogue du vent et de la mer
A stormy exchange between wind and sea.
facts: Debussy said he had once planned a career as a sailor.
The first edition’s cover showed Hokusai’s ‘Great Wave’.
It was mostly written far from the sea.

L122.about: An orchestral triptych: ‘Gigues’, with its rueful English flavour, ‘Ibéria’, a vivid three-part picture of Spain, and ‘Rondes de printemps’, a spring round dance. The orchestration is lavish and precise, and each piece has a very different character.
L122.ctx: Debussy worked on the Images over several years. ‘Ibéria’, first performed in 1910, is the most famous, and Manuel de Falla praised its evocation of Spanish nights. ‘Gigues’ uses an English folk tune and the rare oboe d’amore. The complete triptych was first performed in January 1913. The set is dedicated to Emma Bardac, Debussy’s second wife.
parts: A melancholy English-flavoured dance with an oboe d’amore.
‘Par les rues et par les chemins’, ‘Les parfums de la nuit’ and ‘Le matin d’un jour de fête’.
A spring round dance full of fresh, bright colours.
facts: ‘Gigues’ features the oboe d’amore.
‘Ibéria’ is in three linked sections.
Dedicated to Emma Bardac.

L126.about: A ballet score about a game of tennis, in which a young man and two young women flirt among the trees at dusk. The music is fluid, shifting and very modern, with delicate orchestral colours and a constantly changing rhythmic surface that avoids conventional dance forms.
L126.ctx: Commissioned by Sergei Diaghilev for the Ballets Russes, Jeux was choreographed by Vaslav Nijinsky. It was first performed on 15 May 1913, two weeks before Stravinsky’s Rite of Spring, and was quickly overshadowed by it. Debussy reportedly thought little of the scenario, but the score is now recognised as one of his most daring works.
facts: First performed two weeks before The Rite of Spring.
Choreographed by Nijinsky.
The scenario ends with the sound of an aeroplane crash.

L103.about: Two dances for harp and strings, one solemn and archaic, the other lilting and secular. The solo harp is heard in delicate, veiled colours against the strings.
L103.ctx: Debussy wrote the work for the chromatic harp, a pedal-less instrument developed by the firm of Pleyel as a rival to the pedal harp. It is now usually played on a pedal harp. The premiere was in Paris in November 1904.
facts: Written for the Pleyel chromatic harp.
The two dances are played without a break.
Today it is usually played on the pedal harp.

L85.about: Debussy’s only string quartet, and his only work to carry an opus number. It is cast in four movements linked by a single theme, in a modal G minor with unusual rhythmic freedom and colour. A pizzicato scherzo, a tender slow movement and a passionate finale make up the work.
L85.ctx: Composed in 1892–93 and premiered by the Ysaÿe Quartet in Paris in December 1893, the quartet was dedicated to them. It shows the influence of César Franck’s cyclic technique, but its colour and rhythm are distinctively Debussy’s own. Ravel’s quartet of 1903 was modelled on it, and Debussy encouraged him to leave it untouched.
parts: A cyclic theme opens the quartet.
A rhythmic scherzo with plucked strings.
A passionate finale that recalls the opening theme.
facts: Debussy’s only work with an opus number.
Dedicated to the Ysaÿe Quartet.
Ravel’s quartet was modelled on it.

L135.about: A concise sonata for cello and piano in three movements, all in D minor: a solemn Prologue, a Sérénade that has a Spanish colour, and a quick, nervous Finale. It is wry, brilliant and full of unusual cello effects.
L135.ctx: Debussy wrote it in a few weeks in July 1915 at Pourville on the Normandy coast, as the first of a planned set of six sonatas for various instruments. He completed only three before his death. After early performances in London and Geneva in 1916, the French premiere was given in Paris in 1917 by Joseph Salmon and Debussy himself. He dedicated the sonatas to his wife, Emma.
parts: A solemn opening in the style of a French overture.
A quick, nervous finale in rondo form.
facts: The first of Debussy’s planned six sonatas.
All three movements are in D minor.
The London premiere was on 4 March 1916.

L140.about: Debussy’s last completed major work: a concise, mercurial sonata in three movements, fantastical and unpredictable, with the violin often sounding like a Spanish guitar or a folk fiddle. The ending is brilliant and abrupt.
L140.ctx: It was the third of the six sonatas Debussy planned, written when he was seriously ill with cancer and with France at war. Debussy himself played the piano at the premiere in May 1917, his last public appearance. He described the work as showing what an invalid’s mind can produce in wartime.
facts: Debussy’s last completed major work.
He played the piano at the premiere, his last public appearance.
The third of his planned six sonatas.

L137.about: A sonata for the unusual trio of flute, viola and harp, with a lyrical Pastorale, a graceful Interlude in the manner of a minuet, and a lively Finale. The mixture of timbres gives a delicate, silvery sound, and the melancholy is often veiled with irony.
L137.ctx: The second of Debussy’s planned six sonatas, written in 1915 at Pourville. Debussy said the music was terribly sad and that he did not know whether one should laugh or cry. The unusual combination has since become a favourite for later composers.
facts: The second of Debussy’s six planned sonatas.
Debussy said he did not know whether one should laugh or cry.
The combination has inspired later trios.

L129.about: A short solo for flute, evoking the god Pan playing his pipes after the nymph Syrinx has been transformed into reeds. Its sinuous, modal melody is unaccompanied and fades into silence, and it is among the best-loved works in the flute repertoire.
L129.ctx: Debussy wrote it as ‘Flûte de Pan’ in 1913, as incidental music for Gabriel Mourey’s play Psyché. The flautist Louis Fleury held the exclusive right to perform it until his death in 1926, and it was published in 1927. The original manuscript has no breath marks.
facts: Originally called ‘Flûte de Pan’.
Written as incidental music for Mourey’s play Psyché.
Published in 1927, after Fleury’s death.

L136.ded: To the memory of Frédéric Chopin
L136.about: Twelve studies in two books, each devoted to a technical problem: fingers, thirds, fourths, sixths, octaves, eight fingers, chromatic degrees, ornaments, repeated notes, contrasting sonorities, compound arpeggios and chords. Debussy turns each into a piece of music, with subtle colour and structure.
L136.ctx: Debussy wrote the études in the summer of 1915 at Pourville, while he was editing Chopin’s works for his publisher Durand, and dedicated them to Chopin’s memory. He printed no fingerings, saying that pianists should find those that suit their own hands. The études are among his last piano works.
parts: A playful parody of Czerny’s five-finger exercises.
A study for eight fingers, without thumbs.
facts: Dedicated to the memory of Chopin.
Debussy printed no fingerings.
Written while he was editing Chopin’s music.

L84.about: A song of a glowing evening and the passing of life, set to a poem by Paul Bourget. The vocal line is lyrical and gently flowing over a simple piano accompaniment, and the mood is tender and wistful.
L84.ctx: One of Debussy’s earliest and most popular songs, ‘Beau soir’ is often arranged for violin and piano or for other instruments. It shows the young composer’s gift for setting French verse.
facts: Sets a poem by Paul Bourget.
Often arranged for violin and piano.
One of Debussy’s earliest popular songs.

L29.about: A playful song after Verlaine’s poem, its piano accompaniment imitating strummed mandolins as stock characters of the commedia dell’arte serenade their beloveds. The mood is light, witty and elegant.
L29.ctx: Debussy wrote the song in 1882, when he was a student, for the singer Marie-Blanche Vasnier, for whom he wrote many early songs. The poem comes from Verlaine’s Fêtes galantes, which inspired several of his works.
facts: Written in 1882 when Debussy was a student.
Sets a poem from Verlaine’s Fêtes galantes.
The piano imitates strummed mandolins.

L80.about: Three Verlaine songs of amorous masquerade: the hushed ‘En sourdine’, the comic ‘Fantoches’ and the moonlit ‘Clair de lune’. The vocal writing is delicate and the piano accompaniments are subtle and graceful.
L80.ctx: Debussy set several poems from Verlaine’s Fêtes galantes. His song ‘Clair de lune’ from this set shares its title, and its source, with the famous piano piece of the Suite bergamasque.
parts: A quick, comic scene with stock characters.
facts: ‘Clair de lune’ shares its title with the famous piano piece.
All three poems are by Verlaine.
Debussy later wrote a second set.

L62.about: A lyric poem for two solo voices, women’s chorus and orchestra, based on Dante Gabriel Rossetti’s ‘The Blessed Damozel’ in a French translation. It portrays a heavenly maiden who longs for her earthly lover, and the music is soft, luminous and gently modal.
L62.ctx: Debussy composed it as one of the works he was required to send back to Paris while a Prix de Rome winner. The first performance in April 1893 showed the influence of Wagner and Franck, but also the beginnings of his own style.
L62.sc: Soprano, mezzo-soprano, women’s chorus and orchestra
facts: Based on Rossetti’s ‘The Blessed Damozel’.
Written while Debussy held the Prix de Rome.
First performed in April 1893.

L88.about: Debussy’s only completed opera, a hushed and mysterious drama after Maeterlinck’s symbolist play about the doomed love of Pelléas and Mélisande and the jealousy of her husband Golaud. The vocal lines follow the rhythms of speech, and the orchestra creates atmosphere and psychological depth rather than set-piece arias.
L88.ctx: Debussy began work after seeing Maeterlinck’s play in 1893 and spent nearly a decade completing the score. The first performance took place at the Opéra-Comique on 30 April 1902 and was a landmark of modern French opera. Maeterlinck was angry at the casting and disowned the production.
parts: Golaud finds Mélisande lost in a forest.
Mélisande lets down her long hair from the tower.
Pelléas and Mélisande declare their love; Golaud’s violence.
facts: Debussy’s only completed opera.
Premiered at the Opéra-Comique in 1902.
Based on a play by Maeterlinck.

L117/1.about: ‘The Dancers of Delphi’ is a slow, sculptural piece of solemn, sustained chords that suggests the graceful, stately movements of dancers on an ancient Greek relief. Its simple melody and mild archaic harmony give it a serene, ritual quality.
L117/1.ctx: Composed in 1909–10 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 1, the piece is thought to have been inspired by a sculpture of dancers from Delphi that Debussy had seen. It opens the set with an image of classical antiquity.
facts: The first prélude of Book 1.
Debussy printed the titles at the end of each prélude.
Suggests the dancers of an ancient Greek relief.

L117/2.about: ‘Voiles’ is built on the whole-tone scale, with a short pentatonic middle section, and drifts in soft, hovering harmonies. The French word can mean either ‘sails’ or ‘veils’, and Debussy never said which he meant.
L117/2.ctx: Composed in 1909–10 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 1, the piece is one of Debussy’s clearest examples of whole-tone harmony. Its stillness and ambiguity of title have made it a favourite for pianists and commentators.
facts: ‘Voiles’ can mean ‘sails’ or ‘veils’.
Built largely on the whole-tone scale.
Has a short pentatonic middle section.

L117/3.about: ‘The Wind in the Plain’ is a quick, whispering piece of restless, swirling figuration, with a small melodic figure that hovers above the flowing texture. It sounds like wind sweeping across an open landscape.
L117/3.ctx: Composed in 1909–10 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 1, the piece captures the movement of the air in a texture of continuous, shimmering motion.
facts: Marked ‘Animé’.
Built on a constantly moving texture.
The third prélude of Book 1.

L117/4.about: ‘Sounds and Perfumes Turn in the Evening Air’ is a slow, dreamy waltz-like piece that weaves fragments of melody through drifting harmonies. Debussy takes the title from a line of Baudelaire, whose poem ‘Harmonie du soir’ describes scents and sounds blending together.
L117/4.ctx: Composed in 1909–10 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 1, the piece takes its title from Baudelaire’s poem ‘Harmonie du soir’ in Les Fleurs du mal, a celebrated example of synaesthesia in verse.
facts: The title is a line from Baudelaire’s ‘Harmonie du soir’.
Marked ‘Modéré’.
Has a waltz-like sway.

L117/5.about: ‘The Hills of Anacapri’ is a bright, sunny piece full of dance rhythms, echoes of a tarantella and snatches of folk-like melody, evoking the Italian island of Capri. It is one of the most extrovert of the préludes.
L117/5.ctx: Composed in 1909–10 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 1, the piece portrays a place on the island of Capri with lively Neapolitan colour and a sense of holiday festivity.
facts: Evokes the hills of Anacapri on the island of Capri.
Marked ‘Très modéré’.
Full of tarantella-like rhythms.

L117/6.about: ‘Footprints in the Snow’ is bleak and slow, built on a steady, plodding rhythm like footsteps that persist through a cold, still landscape. A sad, sparse melody drifts over the frozen texture.
L117/6.ctx: Composed in 1909–10 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 1, the piece carries a marking from Debussy asking that the rhythm should have ‘the sonorous value of a sad and frozen landscape’.
facts: Marked ‘Triste et lent’.
Debussy asked for the rhythm to suggest a sad, frozen landscape.
One of the most desolate of the préludes.

L117/7.about: ‘What the West Wind Saw’ is a stormy, tumultuous piece with wild, sweeping figures and violent contrasts. It is one of the most virtuosic and dramatic of the Book 1 préludes.
L117/7.ctx: Composed in 1909–10 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 1, the piece is a burst of raw energy in a set otherwise known for delicate, atmospheric writing.
facts: Marked ‘Animé et tumultueux’.
One of the most turbulent préludes.
Demands considerable technique.

L117/8.about: Titled ’The Girl with the Flaxen Hair’, one of Debussy’s most tender and immediately accessible works, its gentle melody inspired by a poem of the same name by Leconte de Lisle depicting a young woman in a summer meadow.
L117/8.ctx: Composed in 1909–10 as the eighth of the twelve préludes of Book 1, part of Debussy’s mature practice of giving each prelude an evocative title, printed unusually at the end rather than the beginning of the score, so as not to constrain the performer’s imagination in advance.
facts: Its title comes from a poem by Leconte de Lisle.
One of the most frequently performed and recorded of all Debussy’s piano works.
Debussy printed the evocative titles of his préludes at the end of each piece, not the beginning.

L117/9.about: ‘The Interrupted Serenade’ imitates a Spanish guitar serenade that keeps being disturbed by abrupt outbursts, with plucked strumming figures and fleeting, quiet melodies. The humour is dry and precise.
L117/9.ctx: Composed in 1909–10 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 1, the piece is a comic scene, in which a serenading singer is repeatedly interrupted.
facts: Imitates a Spanish guitar.
Full of abrupt interruptions.
The ninth prélude of Book 1.

L117/10.about: Titled ’The Sunken Cathedral’, inspired by a Breton legend of a cathedral that rises from the sea at dawn, its bells and chant audible before it sinks once more beneath the waves. Built on massive, bell-like parallel chords and a slowly unfolding sense of scale, it is one of Debussy’s most vividly pictorial works.
L117/10.ctx: Composed in 1909–10 as the tenth of the Book 1 préludes, drawing on the medieval legend of the drowned city of Ys, whose cathedral was said to reappear periodically from beneath the sea off the coast of Brittany.
facts: Inspired by a Breton legend of a cathedral that rises from the sea.
Built on massive, bell-like parallel chords.
One of the most pictorially vivid of Debussy’s twenty-four préludes.

L117/11.about: ‘The Dance of Puck’ is a quick, capricious piece full of leaps, sudden pauses and mocking flourishes, like the mischievous sprite of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. It is marked ‘Capricieux et léger’.
L117/11.ctx: Composed in 1909–10 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 1, the piece is often linked to the illustrations by Arthur Rackham for A Midsummer Night’s Dream, published in 1908.
facts: Marked ‘Capricieux et léger’.
Portrays Puck from A Midsummer Night’s Dream.
Often linked to Arthur Rackham’s illustrations.

L117/12.about: ‘Minstrels’ is a jaunty, humorous piece in the style of the music-hall entertainers that Debussy saw in Paris, with banjo-like strums, drum-like rhythms and cakewalk syncopation. It ends the first book with a laugh.
L117/12.ctx: Composed in 1909–10 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 1, the piece draws on the American minstrel shows that toured European music halls, a genre now recognised as bound up with racial caricature. Debussy’s music is a light, sophisticated parody.
facts: Marked ‘Nerveux et avec humour’.
Closes Book 1.
Draws on music-hall entertainment popular in Paris.

L123/1.about: ‘Mists’ is a hazy, hushed piece in which the two hands play in different keys, one on the white notes and the other on the black notes, giving a faint, veiled, blurred sound. It opens the second book with a sense of mystery.
L123/1.ctx: Composed in 1912–13 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 2, the piece is an early example of bitonality in Debussy’s work, used to create atmosphere rather than dissonance.
facts: Uses two different keys at once.
The first prélude of Book 2.
Marked ‘Modéré’.

L123/2.about: ‘Dead Leaves’ is slow and melancholy, with sad, falling motifs and colours of autumn. Its mood is one of quiet resignation.
L123/2.ctx: Composed in 1912–13 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 2, the piece uses whole-tone and modal colours to suggest leaves falling and drifting.
facts: Marked ‘Lent et mélancolique’.
The second prélude of Book 2.
Its mood is autumnal.

L123/3.about: ‘The Wine Gate’ is a habanera-rhythm piece in which sudden contrasts of violence and sweetness alternate, capturing the heat and drama of southern Spain. It is a vivid picture of a place Debussy had not visited.
L123/3.ctx: Composed in 1912–13 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 2, the piece was inspired by a postcard of the Puerta del Vino in the Alhambra that Manuel de Falla sent him.
facts: Inspired by a postcard sent by Manuel de Falla.
Marked ‘Mouvement de Habanera’.
Shows Debussy’s imaginative Spain.

L123/4.about: ‘Fairies Are Exquisite Dancers’ is a light, quick piece full of fluttering figures and dainty movement. It is one of Debussy’s most delicate and gossamer pieces.
L123/4.ctx: Composed in 1912–13 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 2, the piece takes its title from a caption to an illustration by Arthur Rackham in Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens.
facts: The title comes from an Arthur Rackham illustration.
Marked ‘Rapide et léger’.
The fourth prélude of Book 2.

L123/5.about: ‘Heather’ is a calm, pastoral piece with a gentle, folk-like melody over quiet harmony. Its peaceful, open sound suggests a stretch of heathland.
L123/5.ctx: Composed in 1912–13 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 2, the piece offers a moment of quiet simplicity between more elaborate pieces in the set.
facts: Marked ‘Calme’.
The fifth prélude of Book 2.
Folk-like in character.

L123/6.about: ‘General Lavine — eccentric’ is a portrait in cakewalk rhythm of a stiff-jointed, puppet-like clown. The music is spiky, witty and full of jerky gestures.
L123/6.ctx: Composed in 1912–13 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 2, the piece pictures Edward La Vine, an American comic entertainer who performed in Paris in 1910. Debussy marks it ‘in the style and tempo of a cakewalk’.
facts: Depicts an American clown who performed in Paris.
Marked as a cakewalk.
One of the funniest préludes.

L123/7.about: ‘The Terrace of Moonlit Audiences’ is a slow, languid piece with exotic, silvery harmonies and a sense of vast, quiet space. Its unusual title suggests an imperial ceremony bathed in moonlight.
L123/7.ctx: Composed in 1912–13 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 2, the title is drawn from a newspaper account of the 1911 Delhi Durbar, where King George V was proclaimed Emperor of India.
facts: The title comes from a report on the 1911 Delhi Durbar.
Marked ‘Lent’.
Among the most exotic of the préludes.

L123/8.about: ‘Ondine’ is a light, quick piece full of splashing figures and flickering arpeggios. It portrays a playful, capricious water sprite.
L123/8.ctx: Composed in 1912–13 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 2, the piece is thought to have been inspired by Arthur Rackham’s illustration for Fouqué’s tale Undine.
facts: Depicts a water sprite.
Marked ‘Scherzando’.
Thought to be inspired by Rackham’s illustrations.

L123/9.about: ‘Homage to S. Pickwick Esq., P.P.M.P.C.’ is a comic, pompous portrait of Dickens’s hero, with a quotation of ‘God Save the King’ and stiff, marching gestures. Its humour is very English.
L123/9.ctx: Composed in 1912–13 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 2, the piece pays tribute to Charles Dickens’s The Pickwick Papers. The letters P.P.M.P.C. stand for ‘Perpetual President, Member Pickwick Club’.
facts: Quotes ‘God Save the King’.
P.P.M.P.C. stands for ‘Perpetual President, Member Pickwick Club’.
A tribute to Dickens.

L123/10.about: ‘Canopus’ is a grave, slow piece of quiet, archaic harmony that evokes an ancient Egyptian funeral urn. Its stillness has a solemn, mysterious quality.
L123/10.ctx: Composed in 1912–13 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 2, the title refers to a canopic jar, which was used by the ancient Egyptians to hold the organs of the dead. Debussy is said to have owned one.
facts: Named after an Egyptian canopic jar.
Marked ‘Très calme et doucement triste’.
The tenth prélude of Book 2.

L123/11.about: ‘Alternating Thirds’ is a quick, sparkling study built entirely on alternating thirds, in the manner of a concert étude. It is brilliant, light and technically demanding.
L123/11.ctx: Composed in 1912–13 as one of the twelve préludes of Book 2, the piece anticipates the Douze Études that Debussy would write in 1915, treating a single technical problem as a musical subject.
facts: A study in alternating thirds.
Anticipates the Douze Études.
Marked ‘Modérément animé’.

L123/12.about: Titled ’Fireworks’, a dazzling, virtuosic depiction of a fireworks display, closing the second book of préludes with a shimmering explosion of colour that quotes a fragment of the French national anthem, ’La Marseillaise’, in its closing bars, as though heard drifting from a distant Bastille Day celebration.
L123/12.ctx: Composed in 1912–13 as the last of the twelve préludes of Book 2, written on the eve of the First World War, a period when Debussy’s health and personal finances were both increasingly precarious.
facts: Closes the second book of préludes with a quotation from ’La Marseillaise’.
Depicts a fireworks display, likely for the French national holiday, Bastille Day.
Among the most technically demanding of Debussy’s twenty-four préludes.
